The Delaware River. Flowing approximately three hundred thirty miles from the Catskill Mountains of New York to Delaware Bay and the Atlantic Ocean, the Delaware forms the boundary between New York and Pennsylvania and between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Though modest in length, it has been historically significant for early American settlement, commerce, and the founding of the nation. The river originates in the Catskill Mountains of southeastern New York from two main branches that converge near Hancock. It flows generally southeastward, serving as the boundary between several northeastern states for most of its course. The river was named after Thomas West, Lord De La Warr, the early colonial governor of Virginia, though the river itself runs through the Mid-Atlantic region. It was historically crucial for shipping, mills, and early settlements, with Philadelphia and Trenton developing on or near its banks as major colonial and early American cities. The Delaware is famous as the site of George Washington's crossing during the American Revolutionary War in seventeen seventy-six, a turning point in the conflict. Further downstream the river forms a relatively narrow and scenic gorge through the Appalachian region known as the Delaware Water Gap, now a major recreational destination. After significant pollution in the twentieth century, restoration efforts have improved water quality and habitat, though the industrial legacy persists.
